prompt.context: Our client is Rotisserie Ranch, a poultry farming company that specializes in growing chickens for rotisserie roasting. Its main line customer segment is comprised of large grocery chains, who buy its chickens to fresh roast in the meat departments of their grocery stores. Market research has revealed to Rotisserie Ranch that more and more consumers have begun buying flavored rotisserie chickens recently.
prompt.question: Rotisserie Ranch is thinking of pre-flavoring some of its chickens for grocers. Should Rotisserie Ranch begin selling this new product?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors in this new product space?
clarifying_info.a: Rotisserie Ranch will only compete against existing Private Label brands at grocery stores. Competition freezes chicken so cannot pre-season it.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have any competitive advantage?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Rotisserie Ranch has a patented process for sterilely packaging chicken so it remains fresh for 30 days, making freezing unnecessary. They are currently the industry market share leader in rotisserie-ready chicken.
Four new flavored products to be introduced concurrently: Barbecue, lemon herb, tandori, and teriyaki.

clarifying_info.q: What happens to unsold cooked chickens?
clarifying_info.a: Predicting demand for cooked chickens is difficult for grocers. Any leftover cooked chickens at the end of the day are thrown out. Unthawed chickens cannot be re-frozen.

exhibits.title: Market Test of Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken
exhibits.shows: A price-quantity chart showing results of a test market for Rotisserie Ranch Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken. Two data points are plotted: Store A and Store B, with retailer margin noted for each.

exhibits.title: Control Group Stores
exhibits.shows: A table comparing Standard Rotisserie and Store-Seasoned Rotisserie chicken across two control stores (Store 1 and Store 2), including weekly sales, retail price, seasoning cost, and retailer margin. Retailer margin for seasoned rotisserie is shown as unknown (?)

framework: Value to customers (grocery chains) — will they buy the pre-seasoned product?
Revenue and cost implications — does the price increase to grocers offset the cost increase to client?
Competition — who else is in the pre-seasoned space and what is their ability to respond?
Market testing — how can we validate demand before a full rollout?

questions.prompt: Do you think that grocery retailers would be interested in pre-seasoned chickens from Rotisserie Ranch?
questions.guidance: No single correct answer; candidate should defend logically. Strong YES arguments: labor cost reduction for meat department workers, economies of scale through seasoning centralization, product consistency via centralized R&D. Strong NO arguments: loss of differentiation (grocery chains differentiate by value-added services), grocers are better attuned to local consumer tastes, increases inventory complexity and SKU count.

questions.prompt: Grocers are interested but want to be sure the chickens will sell well. How would you make sure?
questions.guidance: The correct answer is to run a test market. Candidate should articulate: (1) run a pilot/test market, and (2) the pilot needs a control or comparison group to isolate the effect of the new product.

questions.prompt: A test market launch for the new Rotisserie Ranch BBQ chicken was administered (hand out Exhibit 1). Should the grocers carry our product?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate gross profit for the grocer at each price point using Exhibit 1, then recognize they cannot answer without a control group and ask for Exhibit 2. With both exhibits, candidate calculates variable margin and gross profit for both chicken types and compares. An excellent candidate will also interpolate a mid-point price using the linear demand assumption and note percentage profit improvements.

math.setup: Exhibit 1: Retail margin = 25%. Gross Profit (Grocer) = Retail Margin ($) x Quantity. Exhibit 2: Retailer Margin = 30%, but seasoning cost must be subtracted. Variable Margin ($) = 30% x Retail Price - Seasoning Cost. Gross Profit = Variable Margin x Units Sold (derived from Weekly Sales / Retail Price).
steps: Exhibit 1 — Store A: Retail Margin ($) = 25% x $4.00 = $1.00/unit; Gross Profit = $1.00 x 400 = $400
Exhibit 1 — Store B: Retail Margin ($) = 25% x $3.00 = $0.75/unit; Gross Profit = $0.75 x 1,000 = $750
Exhibit 2 — Standard Rotisserie, Store 1: Variable Margin = 30% x $3.33 - $0.00 = $1.00/unit; Units = $1,000/$3.33 = 300; Gross Profit = $1.00 x 300 = $300
Exhibit 2 — Standard Rotisserie, Store 2: Variable Margin = 30% x $2.50 - $0.00 = $0.75/unit; Units = $2,000/$2.50 = 800; Gross Profit = $0.75 x 800 = $600

Exhibit 2 — Seasoned Rotisserie, Store 1: Variable Margin = 30% x $3.99 - $0.20 = $1.00/unit (same as standard); Units = $1,200/$3.99 = ~300 (comparable to Store 1 standard); Gross Profit = $1.00 x 400 = $400 (vs $300 standard — incremental $100)

Exhibit 2 — Seasoned Rotisserie, Store 2: Variable Margin = 30% x $2.99 - $0.15 = $0.75/unit (same as standard); Units = $2,400/$2.99 = ~800 (comparable to Store 2 standard); Gross Profit = $0.75 x 1,000 = $750 (vs $600 standard — incremental $150)
Bonus — Linear demand interpolation at $3.50: Q = 700 units; Variable Margin = 25% x $3.50 = $0.875/unit; Total Operating Profit = $0.875 x 700 = $612.50
Bonus — % improvement: Store 1 gains $100/$300 = 33.3%; Store 2 gains $150/$600 = 25%
math.answer: Grocers can expect $100–$150 more gross profit per store per week using Rotisserie Ranch pre-seasoned product vs. their own private-label seasoned chicken. Variable margins are identical ($1.00 and $0.75 respectively) but volume is higher for the Rotisserie Ranch product. Cannibalization is not an issue because margins are the same on standard and seasoned rotisserie.

recommendation: Rotisserie Ranch should launch the Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken product and test the other three flavors (lemon herb, tandori, teriyaki) in additional markets.
Competitive necessity: consumers are shifting to seasoned rotisserie chicken and the market is moving in this direction.
Benefit to grocers: assuming the test market is representative, grocers can expect $100–$150 more gross profit per week per store vs. private label.
Benefit to client: the increased price to grocers offsets the increased cost of production, generating more revenue on higher unit volumes.
Cannibalization risk is minimal: variable margins and gross profits are the same on standard and seasoned rotisserie chicken, so any shift to the new product is a net benefit.
risks: Test market may not be fully representative of all store types or geographies.
Cannibalization of existing standard rotisserie chicken volumes if demand does not grow additively.
Grocers may resist outsourcing seasoning if they value differentiation or local flavor customization.
Scaling the patented sterile packaging process may introduce production costs not captured in the test.
next_steps: Run test markets for the three remaining flavors (lemon herb, tandori, teriyaki) with proper control groups.
Assess whether increased production costs are fully offset by price uplift at each flavor tier.
Evaluate potential scale benefits as pre-seasoned volumes grow over time.
Quantify labor reduction savings for grocers as seasoning workload is outsourced to Rotisserie Ranch.
